overview.intro: This lesson teaches how to prevent contamination during daily clinical work, from routine exam-room turnover through injections, catheter placement, wound care, isolation, and surgery. Infection prevention is not a single task; it is a chain of small decisions that protect Pets, Members, and team members. AAHA frames infection control, prevention, and biosecurity as central to veterinary care because a single breach can undo the team’s best work, and calls for written SOPs, training, surveillance, and compliance evaluation. CDC describes core infection-prevention practices — hand hygiene, environmental cleaning and disinfection, injection safety, PPE risk assessment, reprocessing reusable equipment, transmission-based precautions, and occupational health — as fundamental expectations in every healthcare setting. This lesson is written for new hires and experienced team members alike: PetNurses, Nurse Aides, Pet Practitioners, and DVMs.
objectives: Distinguish medical asepsis, surgical asepsis, cleaning, disinfection, high-level disinfection, and sterilization using practical Hannah examples.

Break the chain of infection by interrupting common transmission routes: hands, gloves, shared equipment, surfaces, instruments, sharps, body fluids, respiratory secretions, and movement through the hospital.
Choose when to wash hands, use alcohol-based hand sanitizer, change gloves, and don PPE based on task risk.
Prepare and reset exam rooms, treatment areas, kennels, procedure areas, and surgical suites without carrying contamination forward.
Follow label- and protocol-based rules for disinfectant selection, dilution, wet contact time, surface compatibility, PPE, ventilation, and storage.
Protect asepsis during injections, IV catheter placement, blood collection, urinary catheterization, wound care, and surgery within your role and under DVM or RVT direction where required.
Open sterile supplies, maintain sterile fields, and respond immediately when sterility is compromised.
Recognize and correct common breaches: touched sterile gloves, reused equipment, shortened contact time, catheter-site contamination, contagious-disease risk, and breaks in surgical sterility.
overview.connectsForward: Medication Safety taught you to verify before you act. Asepsis and Infection Prevention is the other half of every treatment task: it protects the Pet from what you cannot see. The C.L.E.A.N. Path, the hand-hygiene moments, the label rule, and the breach response carry into catheter care, fluid therapy, wound management, dentistry, anesthesia support, surgery, and every hospitalized shift. If you are unsure whether something is clean or sterile, stop and ask. Protecting every Pet begins with preventing contamination.

modules.title: Why Asepsis Matters at Hannah
modules.completionBody: You have the shared language and the C.L.E.A.N. Path. Continue to medical versus surgical asepsis.
modules.content:
Asepsis means preventing contamination. At Hannah it protects every Pet, every Member, and every team member. A Pet can arrive with an infection, develop one during care, or carry organisms that spread through hands, surfaces, equipment, shared supplies, or droplets. AAHA states that the veterinary team’s best work can be undone by a breach in infection control, prevention, and biosecurity (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Explain why infection prevention is clinical care, not housekeeping.
  • Name the spaces where asepsis applies — every one of them.
  • Recite the Hannah C.L.E.A.N. Path and use it as a pause before, during, and after a task.
  • Spot contamination risks on a real treatment table and say what you would change.

Why it matters

Infection prevention is a chain of small decisions

Infection prevention is not one task. It is a chain of small decisions: what you touch, what you clean first, what you change, what you wait for, and what you say when something looks wrong. CDC describes core infection-prevention practices as fundamental expectations in every healthcare setting, including hand hygiene, environmental cleaning and disinfection, injection safety, PPE risk assessment, reprocessing reusable equipment, and transmission-based precautions (CDC core practices).

It is also occupational safety. Veterinary standard precautions exist to reduce zoonotic transmission and occupational exposure for the people doing the work (NASPHV veterinary infection prevention and control).

Every role is included. PetNurses, Nurse Aides, Pet Practitioners, and DVMs all work inside the same chain. Credential and role determine who performs a procedure; they never determine who is allowed to speak up.

Where asepsis applies

Lobby handoff, exam room, treatment area, kennel, lab, pharmacy, procedure room, surgical suite, isolation.

What moves contamination

Hands, gloves, shared equipment, surfaces, pockets, linens, waste, sharps, and the path you walk.

What protects the Pet

Hand hygiene, cleaning before disinfecting, label contact time, barriers, dedicated equipment, sterile technique.

What stops a breach

Any team member, at any moment, saying: I think this may be contaminated. Let us pause and check.

The framework

The Hannah C.L.E.A.N. Path

The C.L.E.A.N. Path is a memory framework for asepsis education, not a medical claim and not a substitute for protocol. It gives every role the same five-beat pause before, during, and after a clinical task.

Check the risk. Lower the load. Establish barriers. Apply the rule. Never carry contamination forward.

The C.L.E.A.N. Path step explorer

Step explorer

Open each letter to see what it means in practice. Arrow keys move between letters; every step you open is marked as viewed.

C — Check the risk

What could be infectious, sterile, sharp, or chemical here?

  • Pet status: routine visit, wound, vomiting or diarrhea, respiratory signs, skin lesions, isolation concern.
  • Task status: clean, dirty, aseptic, sterile, invasive, sharps involved, chemical involved.
  • Space status: exam room, treatment area, kennel, lab, pharmacy, procedure room, surgical suite, isolation.
  • Standard precautions apply to every Pet, and PPE is chosen by risk assessment, not by habit.
L — Lower the load

What needs cleaning before anything is disinfected or sterilized?

  • Remove waste, linens, used supplies, and visible soil first.
  • Clean before you disinfect and before anything is sterilized.
  • Keep used instruments contained and processed promptly so soil does not dry on them.
  • Dried organic material is harder to remove and can make later processing less effective.
E — Establish barriers

What protects the Pet, the team, and the field?

  • Hand hygiene at the right moments, then the gloves and PPE the task calls for.
  • Dedicated equipment, or cleaned and disinfected equipment, between Pets.
  • Drapes, sterile packaging, sharps containers at point of use, traffic control, isolation signage.
  • PPE is the last barrier, not the only one: workflow, layout, and protocol come first.
A — Apply the rule

What does the label, the protocol, or DVM or RVT direction require?

  • Product label and SDS: dilution, wet contact time, PPE, ventilation, surface, storage.
  • Hannah protocol: room reset, kennel sequence, isolation, surgery, catheter, wound, waste.
  • State and local rules for regulated medical waste and sharps.
  • DVM or RVT direction for procedure-specific prep and for anything role-restricted.
N — Never carry contamination forward

What do I change, discard, disinfect, or report before moving on?

  • Change gloves and clean hands before touching anything clean.
  • Replace contaminated sterile items instead of correcting them yourself.
  • Finish the full wet contact time; re-prep or re-clean if something was touched, soiled, or dried early.
  • Dispose of sharps at point of use, then report the breach so the team can correct the system.
Clean zone

Clean and sterile supplies, medication preparation, prepared sterile fields, restocked surfaces.

Contaminated zone

Used instruments, waste and sharps, soiled linens, sinks and drains, used PPE, anything a used glove touched.

Find the contamination risk — treatment table

Contamination spotting

Eight items on and around a treatment table. Flag every one that is a contamination risk, then check your work. Three of them are examples of what right looks like.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask

Every procedural screen in this lesson follows the same order: the universal principle first, then the Hannah protocol and product label that make it specific, then the instruction to ask the DVM, RVT, or lead PetNurse if the next safe step is unclear.

This lesson never gives you a dilution ratio, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule. Those live on the label, in Hannah protocol, and in state and local rules.

modules.title: Medical vs Surgical Asepsis
modules.completionBody: You can separate clean, disinfected, and sterile. Continue to how contamination actually moves.
modules.content:
Clean, disinfected, and sterile are three different states, and mixing up the words is how sterile supplies end up on nonsterile surfaces. This module gives you the shared vocabulary and the risk hierarchy behind it.

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Define medical asepsis, surgical asepsis, cleaning, disinfection, high-level disinfection, and sterilization.
  • Give a Hannah example of each and name the caution that goes with it.
  • Use the Spaulding risk concept to decide how an item must be processed.
  • Treat any sterile item of uncertain status as contaminated.

Two kinds of asepsis

Medical asepsis reduces spread; surgical asepsis protects a sterile field

Medical asepsis is everything you do to reduce the number and spread of microorganisms in routine care: hand hygiene, gloves for a fecal cleanup, disinfecting an exam table, dedicated equipment for a Pet in isolation. Surgical asepsis keeps items and fields free of microorganisms for invasive procedures: sterile gloves, sterile instruments, sterile drapes, sterile catheter supplies, and a monitored sterile field (NCBI Bookshelf — aseptic technique; OpenStax — sterile technique).

The practical rule that separates them: clean is not sterile, and if sterility is broken or uncertain, the team treats the item as contaminated and replaces or corrects it according to protocol.

Cleaning — remove the soil

Removes visible soil, organic matter, and debris. It always comes first: CDC recommends meticulous cleaning before high-level disinfection or sterilization, and notes that dried material is harder to remove and makes processing less effective (CDC disinfection and sterilization recommendations).

Disinfection — kill many or most

A chemical process on inanimate surfaces that kills many or most microorganisms, depending on product and level. The label governs dilution, wet contact time, PPE, ventilation, surface, and storage (EPA pesticide labels).

High-level disinfection — for items touching mucous membranes

Generally the minimum for semicritical items that contact mucous membranes or non-intact skin. FDA clears liquid chemical sterilants and high-level disinfectants for specific device uses (FDA sterilants and high-level disinfectants).

Sterilization — destroy all microorganisms

Required for critical items entering sterile tissue or the vascular system. Sterility depends on correct cleaning, packaging, processing, storage, and handling (CDC rational approach).

The Spaulding risk concept in one line

Critical items enter sterile tissue or the vascular system and must be sterile. Semicritical items contact mucous membranes or non-intact skin and generally need high-level disinfection at minimum. Noncritical items contact intact skin and are usually cleaned or low-level disinfected based on risk (CDC rational approach).

The level always follows the item’s use, the manufacturer instructions, and Hannah protocol — not convenience.

Sort by required level

Level sort

Twelve items from a Hannah hospital. Select an item, then move it to the level it needs. Some items depend on how they are used — read the reason on each card after you check.

Unsorted items — select one, then choose a level
Clean first

Visible soil and organic material must come off before anything else happens.

    Clean, then disinfect

    Surfaces and noncritical equipment, per label and protocol.

      Sterile or high-level processed

      Items entering sterile tissue, the vascular system, or contacting mucous membranes.

        Discard

        Single-use items and anything with compromised packaging or sterility.

          • Clean is not sterile

            A team member says the exam table is “sterile” because it was just disinfected. How do you respond?

          • Medical asepsis

            Which of these is a medical-asepsis practice?

          • Surgical asepsis

            During an invasive procedure, a sterile item touches a nonsterile wrapper. What is the status of that item?

            Which item is “critical” under the Spaulding risk concept and must be sterile before use?

modules.title: Chain of Infection and Transmission
modules.completionBody: You can name the six links and the action that breaks each one. Continue to hands, gloves, and PPE.
modules.content:
Contamination moves along a chain with six links. You do not have to remember microbiology to interrupt it — you have to recognize which link you are standing next to and take the action that breaks it.

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Name the six links: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
  • Match each link to the veterinary routes that matter: hands, surfaces, equipment, fluids, secretions, sharps, and traffic.
  • Choose the action that breaks a given link, and explain why the shortcut versions do not.
  • Recognize that breaking any single link can stop transmission.

The chain

Six links, and any one of them will do

An infection needs every link to connect: an agent, a reservoir to live in, a way out, a way to travel, a way in, and a host who is susceptible. Break any link and transmission can stop.

CDC groups the practical break points as hand hygiene, environmental cleaning and disinfection, injection safety, PPE, minimizing exposures, reprocessing reusable equipment, transmission-based precautions, management of temporary invasive devices, and occupational health (CDC core practices). Those are the actions in this activity.

Chain-of-infection transmission breaker

Chain breaker

Select a link to open it, then choose the action that breaks it. Wrong choices explain why the shortcut fails and stay available so you can correct them. Break all six links to finish.

Break the agent link
Break the reservoir link
Break the portal-of-exit link
Break the transmission link
Break the portal-of-entry link
Break the susceptible-host link
Chain broken at all six links

You do not need to know the organism to interrupt transmission. Clean hands, contained sources, processed equipment, full label contact time, protected invasive sites, and early separation break the chain in daily work.

Hands and gloves

The most frequent vehicle in any hospital, and the easiest to interrupt: clean hands and change gloves at the right moments.

Shared equipment

Thermometers, stethoscopes, otoscopes, clippers, monitors, and glucose devices move between Pets unless they are processed or dedicated.

Surfaces and fomites

Tables, handles, keyboards, leashes, carriers, and pockets hold contamination until something removes it.

Traffic and movement

The route you walk a suspected contagious Pet through becomes part of the chain.

One question that catches most breaches

Before you touch the next clean thing, ask: what did my hands, my gloves, or this equipment touch last?

If the answer is a Pet, a body fluid, waste, or a contaminated surface, then hand hygiene, a glove change, or equipment processing comes first — every time.

modules.title: Hands, Gloves, and PPE
modules.completionBody: Hand hygiene moments, glove rules, and PPE selection are the habits everything else rests on. Continue to cleaning, disinfecting, and sterilizing.
modules.content:
Hands are the most common way contamination travels, and the easiest link to break. Gloves help, but only when they are changed at the right moments — and they never replace hand hygiene.

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Name the six hand-hygiene moments in clinical work.
  • Choose soap and water versus alcohol-based hand rub based on whether hands are visibly soiled.
  • Apply the glove rules: clean hands before, change between dirty and clean, change between Pets, hand hygiene after.
  • Select PPE from anticipated exposure and the product label, not from habit.
  • Don and doff PPE in an order that keeps contamination off your hands, clothing, and face.

When to clean your hands

Six moments, in Hannah language

Before touching a Pet. Before an aseptic task, such as handling invasive supplies or assisting with an indwelling device. Before moving from a soiled body site to a clean body site on the same Pet. After touching a Pet or the Pet’s surroundings. After contact with blood, body fluids, waste, contaminated surfaces, or contaminated equipment. And immediately after removing gloves (CDC hand hygiene for healthcare workers).

Which product? CDC states alcohol-based hand rub is preferred in most clinical situations unless hands are visibly soiled; WHO likewise recommends handrub for routine antisepsis when hands are not visibly soiled, and soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or soiled with blood or body fluids (WHO hand hygiene guidelines). Volume and rub time come from the product label and Hannah policy.

The six hand-hygiene moments

Click to reveal

Open each moment to see why it exists and what to do. Reveal all six, or hide them and test yourself.

Before touching a Pet

You are walking up to a Pet you have not touched yet. Why does hand hygiene come first?

You are about to transfer whatever is on your hands to that Pet. Clean hands before Pet contact is a standing CDC clinical indication, regardless of how clean your hands look or when you last washed them.

Do: alcohol-based hand rub if hands are not visibly soiled; soap and water if they are.

Before an aseptic task

You are about to handle invasive supplies or assist with an indwelling device.

Aseptic tasks bypass the Pet’s own barriers, so the hands that prepare them start clean. Hand hygiene comes before the gloves go on.

Do: clean hands, then don the gloves the task requires. Gloves never replace hand hygiene.

Dirty to clean on the same Pet

You are moving from a soiled area to a clean site on the same Pet.

Same Pet still means transfer. The glove or hand that touched the soiled site will carry organisms to the clean one.

Do: hand hygiene and a glove change before you touch the clean site. Wiping gloves does not count.

After touching a Pet or its surroundings

You have finished handling the Pet, the bedding, the carrier, or the run.

The Pet’s surroundings count as the Pet. Bedding, carriers, leashes, and run surfaces are all reservoirs.

Do: hand hygiene before you touch anything clean, including keyboards, handles, and clean supplies.

After blood, body fluids, waste, or contaminated surfaces

You have had contact with blood, body fluids, waste, or a contaminated surface or piece of equipment.

This is the moment where visible soil decides the product for you.

Do: soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or soiled with blood or body fluids; alcohol-based hand rub is preferred in most other clinical moments.

Immediately after removing gloves

The gloves are off. Are your hands clean?

Not necessarily. Hands can be contaminated during glove removal or through defects in the glove itself, which is why CDC lists this as its own indication.

Do: remove gloves carefully to avoid contaminating your hands, then perform hand hygiene immediately.

Hand-hygiene decision path

Decision path

One shift, five moments. Choose the right action at each step and build your hand-hygiene record. Wrong options explain why they are unsafe.

Step 1 — what is on your hands?

You have just cleaned up a diarrhea accident in the kennel run. Your gloves are off. Your hands look visibly soiled. What comes first?

Step 2 — moving to the next task

Hands are clean and dry. You are heading to a routine exam for a different Pet, and your hands are not visibly soiled. What do you use before touching that Pet?

Step 3 — before an aseptic task

The DVM asks you to assist with an IV catheter placement. What is the hand-hygiene moment here?

Step 4 — dirty to clean on the same Pet

You are working on one Pet and move from a soiled area to a clean site on the same Pet. What now?

Step 5 — after the task

Gloves are coming off after the task. What is the last step?

Your hand-hygiene record

Nothing chosen yet. Start with the first step.

    All five moments handled correctly

    Visibly soiled means soap and water. Not visibly soiled means alcohol-based hand rub is preferred in most clinical moments. Before an aseptic task, before touching a clean site on the same Pet, and immediately after glove removal are all their own indications.

    Gloves do not replace hand hygiene

    Clean hands before gloves go on for clean or sterile technique, and clean hands again the moment they come off.

    Change gloves when

    Moving dirty to clean, between Pets, when torn, when heavily contaminated, or before touching any clean surface.

    Gloves are single-use

    No rinsing, no wiping, no reuse. A wiped glove is a redistributed contamination, not a clean glove.

    PPE is the last barrier

    Workflow, layout, traffic control, and protocol come first in the hierarchy of controls; PPE catches what is left.

    Choosing PPE

    Anticipated exposure decides, and the label has a vote

    Select PPE based on what you expect to contact: blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin, contaminated equipment, infectious agents, or chemicals. Gloves for contact, eye or face protection for splash risk, a gown when clothing contamination is likely, and respiratory protection per protocol and risk (CDC core practices).

    PPE works only when it is selected, worn, removed, and disposed of correctly. AAHA warns that incorrect doffing can contaminate hands and surfaces, which is why the order matters (AAHA donning and doffing sequence). And PPE alone is the weakest control: AAHA and NIOSH both put workflow, engineering, and administrative controls above it (AAHA infection control strategies; NIOSH hierarchy of controls).

    PPE selection board

    PPE decisions

    Three situations from one shift. Choose the PPE decision that matches the anticipated exposure. Each answer explains why the alternatives are not appropriate.

    • Routine exam

      A routine wellness exam for a healthy Pet with no wounds and no body-fluid exposure expected. What is the PPE decision?

    • Diarrhea cleanup

      You are cleaning a kennel run for a Pet with acute diarrhea, and splashing is likely during the rinse. What do you select?

    • Suspected contagious respiratory case

      A Pet with acute cough and known exposure to a contagious respiratory illness is being moved per protocol. What guides your PPE?

    Practice complete

    Donning and doffing sequence

    Ordered sequence

    Put the eight steps in order, from clean hands through hand hygiene at the end. A step chosen out of order explains itself and stays available.

    Choose the next correct step
    Your sequence so far
      Sequence complete

      Gloves go on last and come off first. Facial protection comes off last so contaminated hands never travel over your face. Hand hygiene closes the sequence, because doffing itself can contaminate hands. Follow the Hannah and AAHA sequence posted where you work.

  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.

In this module you will

  • Explain why cleaning must come before disinfection or sterilization.
  • Ask the eight disinfectant-selection questions before you pick up a bottle.
  • Read dilution, wet contact time, PPE, ventilation, surface, and storage off the label — never from memory.

Cleaning first

A disinfectant cannot work through soil

Visible soil, organic matter, blood, tissue, feces, and dried material must be removed before disinfection or sterilization. CDC recommends cleaning patient-care items with water and detergent or enzymatic cleaners before high-level disinfection or sterilization, and notes that dried or baked-on material makes removal harder and can make processing less effective or ineffective (CDC disinfection and sterilization recommendations).

That is the L in the C.L.E.A.N. Path: lower the load before you try to kill anything.

Eight questions before you pick up the bottle

1. What organism or risk level are we targeting? 2. Is the surface clean enough for the product to work? 3. Is the product approved for this surface and use site? 4. What dilution does the label require? 5. How long must the surface stay visibly wet? 6. What PPE, ventilation, and storage does the label require? 7. Is it safe for the species in the area and compatible with the material? 8. What does Hannah protocol require?

EPA states pesticide labels are legally enforceable and explain how to handle and use the product safely and legally, and that using a product inconsistently with its labeling violates federal law (EPA pesticide labels). Merck notes veterinary facilities should weigh broad-spectrum efficacy, licensing for animal use, local regulations, and toxicity to Pets and team members (Merck Veterinary Manual). Product lists such as EPA List N exist for specific organism claims (EPA List N).

Wet contact-time simulation

Timer simulation

Contact time is measured in wet time. Choose one of the mock labels below — the required duration comes from the label you pick, not from this lesson and not from any universal number. Then apply, watch, and see what happens if the surface dries or gets wiped early. Real products have their own required times; only your product label is authoritative.

1. Choose a mock product label

2. Watch the surface

Contact time completed as the label required

The surface stayed visibly wet for the full time the label specified. If it dries early, reapply so it stays wet for the full label-required time — do not count the elapsed time as complete, do not add water, and do not wipe it dry to finish faster. The numbers in this simulation are mock values chosen to demonstrate the principle; the real value is on your product label.

Product-label and dilution audit

Label audit

Ten lines from one disinfection task. Flag every line that is not acceptable, then check your audit. Four lines are examples of what right looks like.

Instruments

The flow from point of use to the next opening

At point of use, prevent drying and contain contaminated instruments according to Hannah protocol. Transport them safely. Clean promptly with the correct detergent or enzymatic cleaner. Inspect for debris, damage, and function. Package and sterilize critical instruments per the validated process. And never use a set if contamination or a processing failure is suspected (CDC recommendations; CDC rational approach).

Instrument processing sequence

Ordered sequence

Eight steps from point of use to the next opening. Put them in order; a step chosen too early explains why.

Choose the next correct step
Your sequence so far
    Instrument flow complete

    Contain at point of use, transport safely, clean promptly, inspect, package, sterilize, store dry and intact, and verify at the next opening. Manufacturer instructions and the Hannah sterilizer policy govern the specifics of every step.

    Cleaning and disinfection decisions

    Paged decisions

    Four decisions where the shortcut is tempting. Each answer explains why the alternatives are not appropriate.

    • Cleaning first

      A kennel run has visible organic soil. A team member sprays disinfectant directly over it and moves on. What is wrong?

    • Contact time

      The label requires the surface to stay wet for its contact time. The surface dries halfway through. What do you do?

    • Where the numbers come from

      A new team member asks you what dilution and contact time to use for the treatment-room disinfectant. What is the right answer?

    • Instruments

      A surgical set comes back from a procedure and is stacked dry on a counter until the end of the shift. What is the risk?

    Practice complete

    Chemical safety is part of asepsis

    Disinfectants and sterilants can require PPE, ventilation, SDS review, safe storage, and training. Labels and safety data sheets are how those hazards are communicated (OSHA Hazard Communication), and FDA clears specific liquid chemical sterilants and high-level disinfectants for device use (FDA sterilants and high-level disinfectants).

    If a secondary container is unlabeled, if you cannot find the SDS, or if the required PPE is not available: stop and ask before using the product.

modules.title: Rooms, Kennels, Equipment, and Isolation
modules.completionBody: You can reset a space and run an isolation entry and exit. Continue to Pet skin prep and sterile fields.
modules.content:
Now the principles meet real spaces: exam rooms between Pets, treatment areas where clean and dirty sit too close together, kennels, procedure rooms, surgical suites, and isolation.

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Reset an exam room in the correct order without carrying contamination forward.
  • Keep medication preparation separate from contaminated equipment in the treatment area.
  • Identify the high-touch and Pet-contact surfaces that need attention between Pets.
  • Run an isolation entry and exit using signage, dedicated equipment, and correct doffing.
  • Trigger isolation on suspicion, not on confirmation, and escalate early.
Clean path

Medication preparation area, clean supply storage, restocked surfaces, prepared sterile fields, clean hands and gloves.

Contaminated path

Used equipment, sinks and drains, waste and sharps, soiled linen, used PPE, and any surface a used glove touched.

Exam-room reset sequence

Ordered sequence

Eight steps between Pets. Put them in order. Note where hand hygiene falls — restocking with contaminated gloves is one of the most common breaches.

Choose the next correct step
Your sequence so far
    Room reset complete

    Remove, PPE, clean, disinfect, hold the full label contact time, hand hygiene, restock, reset. If you restock with the gloves you cleaned in, you have just put the contamination onto the clean supplies.

    Surface map — what needs attention between Pets

    Surface map

    Eight surfaces in one exam room. Flag every surface that needs cleaning and disinfection as part of the between-Pets reset. Two of them do not.

    Treatment areas

    Keep the clean path clean

    Keep medication preparation away from contaminated equipment, sinks, waste, and used supplies. Clean and disinfect shared equipment between Pets. Do not place clean supplies on dirty counters or carry them against contaminated clothing. CDC recommends drawing up medications in a designated clean medication preparation area away from potential contamination sources, and cleaning and disinfecting that area regularly and when soiled (CDC injection safety). Shared devices are a documented transmission route and need processing between Pets (CDC shared-device considerations).

    Required scenario 2 — equipment reused without disinfection

    Required scenario

    Choose the safest response. After you choose, the panel explains your answer and why each alternative is not appropriate.

    • Scenario 2 — equipment reused without disinfection

      A team member uses a thermometer and stethoscope on a Pet with diarrhea, then places both on the clean treatment counter for the next Pet without cleaning or disinfection. What is the safest response?

    Practice complete

    Kennels

    Remove, clean, disinfect, and do not move contamination down the row

    Remove the Pet and movable items as appropriate and safe. Remove waste and organic material first. Clean surfaces before disinfecting. Use the correct product and its wet contact time. Avoid moving contaminated tools from kennel to kennel. Use dedicated or disinfected equipment for Pets with diarrhea, respiratory signs, draining wounds, or suspected contagious disease, and escalate outbreak concerns (AAHA ICPB Guidelines; canine diarrhea risk-factor study).

    Required scenario 3 — incorrect disinfectant contact time

    Required scenario

    Choose the safest response. After you choose, the panel explains your answer and why each alternative is not appropriate.

    • Scenario 3 — incorrect disinfectant contact time

      You disinfect an exam table after a coughing Pet. The label or Hannah protocol requires the surface to stay wet for the specified contact time. The disinfectant dries halfway through. What should you do?

    Practice complete

    Procedure areas and surgical suites

    Prepare late, protect always, control the traffic

    Prepare the area before bringing sterile supplies into the field. Open supplies close to the time of use. Limit traffic and unnecessary movement around a sterile setup. If a field is delayed, follow the approved covering and monitoring protocol — AORN guidance emphasizes preparing the sterile field as close as possible to the time of use and using specific covering methods when a field is not used immediately (AORN sterile-technique key takeaways).

    For surgery: confirm room readiness, cleaned surfaces, needed equipment, sterile packs, the traffic plan, and the waste and sharps setup before the Pet enters. Keep sterile fields in sight, dry, above waist level, and protected from nonsterile contact, and remove or replace anything that becomes contaminated (Guidelines in Practice: Sterile Technique).

    Isolation

    Separate early and ask early

    Isolation is a response to suspected or confirmed contagious risk, and it starts on suspicion. Move the Pet according to Hannah triage and isolation protocol. Use the PPE and dedicated equipment the signage and protocol specify. Limit traffic. Handle waste, laundry, and dishes per protocol. Clean and disinfect after contact using the label and Hannah SOP. Escalate to the DVM or RVT if signs change, PPE supply is missing, or a breach occurs.

    CDC states transmission-based precautions should be adapted to the healthcare setting, facility design, and type of patient interaction (CDC isolation precautions; CDC core practices). The isolation category, signage, PPE, and discharge cleaning are set by Hannah protocol and DVM or public-health direction — never by this lesson and never from memory.

    Isolation doorway — entry and exit

    Branching case

    Five decisions from the door in to the door out. Wrong choices explain themselves and stay available so you can correct them.

    Decision 1 — at the door

    A Pet is in the isolation area under Hannah protocol. The signage lists the PPE required for entry. You need to go in to refill water. What do you do first?

    Decision 2 — equipment

    You need a thermometer while you are inside. There is a dedicated one in the isolation area, and a shared one in your pocket.

    Decision 3 — the Pet looks worse

    The Pet’s signs have changed since the last check, and the PPE stock inside the area is running low. What do you do?

    Decision 4 — exit

    You are leaving the isolation area. What is the exit sequence?

    Decision 5 — afterwards

    The Pet is discharged from the isolation area. What happens to the space and the equipment?

    Actions you have taken
      Isolation entry and exit complete

      Signage first, hand hygiene, PPE in order, dedicated equipment that stays inside, immediate escalation for changing signs or missing PPE, correct doffing, and hand hygiene on the way out. Then label-based cleaning and protocol-based waste and laundry handling after discharge.

      Required scenario 5 — suspected contagious disease

      Required scenario

      Choose the first action. After you choose, the panel explains your answer and why each alternative is not appropriate.

      • Scenario 5 — suspected contagious disease

        A Pet arrives with acute vomiting and diarrhea and a recent boarding history. The Member is worried and the Pet is waiting near other Pets. What should you do first?

      Practice complete

      Sources for this module+

      • CDC — Considerations for Blood Glucose Monitoring and Insulin Administration

modules.title: Pet Skin Prep, Sterile Supplies, and Sterile Fields
modules.completionBody: You can protect a prepared site, open sterile supplies safely, read a sterile field, and handle sharps and waste. Continue to fix the breach and the knowledge check.
modules.content:
This module is role-safe by design. It does not give you an antiseptic, a scrub pattern, a contact time, a clip margin, or a number of passes — those come from Hannah protocol and DVM or RVT direction. It teaches the decision points and the contamination rules that apply to every role.

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Protect asepsis during injections, IV catheter placement, blood collection, urinary catheterization, wound care, and surgery within your role.
  • Open sterile supplies without contaminating the contents or the field.
  • Read a sterile field and name every contaminated zone.
  • Respond immediately when sterility is compromised, in words the team can act on.
  • Handle sharps at point of use and separate waste per Hannah and state or local rules.
Injection

Clean hands, prepare medication in a clean designated area, use a new sterile needle and syringe, avoid touching the cleaned site, discard the sharp immediately.

Boundary: Site prep specifics follow the medication instructions, Hannah protocol, and DVM or RVT direction.

IV catheter placement

Treat it as an aseptic task: hand hygiene, clean work area, supplies prepared before restraint, prepared site protected, contaminated supplies replaced.

Boundary: Clipping, antiseptic choice, scrub pattern, and dwell time are Hannah, DVM, or RVT protocol — and placement is role-restricted.

Blood collection

Gloves when blood exposure is anticipated, clean supplies, site prep per protocol, tube and needle contamination prevented, sharps disposed at point of use.

Boundary: Collection site, restraint, and antiseptic are directed by protocol or the DVM or RVT.

Urinary catheterization

Sterile or appropriately processed catheter supplies with aseptic technique; the catheter is protected from every nonsterile surface.

Boundary: Placement is role-specific and DVM or RVT directed.

Wound care

Work clean to dirty, protect clean supplies, use sterile supplies when ordered or when sterile technique is required, change gloves moving from contaminated to clean steps.

Boundary: Wound cleansing solution, debridement, dressing, and medication decisions are DVM or RVT directed.

Surgery

Protect the surgical prep, drapes, sterile instruments, sterile gloves, and the sterile field; report any break immediately.

Boundary: Surgical prep details are procedure-specific and directed by the surgical protocol and the DVM team.

The habit that covers all six

Hand hygiene at the right moment, a clean or sterile work area, supplies prepared before restraint, a prepared site nobody touches, contaminated supplies replaced rather than salvaged, sharps at point of use, and hand hygiene again at the end.

CDC injection safety teaches “One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time” and states that needles and syringes are contaminated after use and must be discarded (CDC injection safety). CDC hand hygiene guidance includes cleaning hands before aseptic tasks and immediately after glove removal (CDC hand hygiene).

Pet skin-prep workflow — assisting with an IV catheter

Workflow builder

Five decisions from before you touch anything through closing out the task. Wrong options explain why they are unsafe and stay available.

Step 1 — before you touch anything

The DVM has asked for an IV catheter placement. You are assisting within your role. What comes first?

Step 2 — the prepared site

The site has been clipped and prepped following Hannah protocol and DVM or RVT direction. What is your rule about that skin now?

Step 3 — something touches the site

While repositioning, a nonsterile finger brushes the prepared insertion site. Nothing has been placed yet.

Step 4 — sharps and supplies

The placement is done. The stylet and the used supplies are in your hand.

Step 5 — closing out

The Pet is settled and the device is in place. What closes the task?

Your aseptic workflow record

Nothing chosen yet. Start with the first step.

    Workflow complete

    Prepare first, protect the prepared site, stop and speak up the moment anything nonsterile touches it, dispose of the sharp at point of use, and close with hand hygiene, documentation, and monitoring. Every variable step — antiseptic, pattern, timing — came from Hannah protocol and DVM or RVT direction, not from this lesson.

    Required scenario 4 — contamination during IV catheter placement

    Required scenario

    Choose the next safe action. After you choose, the panel explains your answer and why each alternative is not appropriate.

    • Scenario 4 — contamination during IV catheter placement

      During IV catheter placement, the site has been clipped and prepped. While repositioning, a nonsterile finger touches the prepared insertion site. What is the next safe action?

    Practice complete

    Opening sterile supplies

    Check it, open it away from you, and never reach over the field

    Check package integrity, the sterility indicator when applicable, expiration when applicable, moisture, tears, punctures, and that it is the correct item. Open on a clean, dry surface at the correct height. Touch only the outside or the nonsterile flaps with nonsterile hands. Present or drop the contents without reaching over the sterile field. OpenStax teaches that the outside of sterile packaging and the 1-inch border are unsterile, and that supplies should be checked and kept within reach before a sterile procedure (OpenStax sterile technique; AORN sterile-technique questions answered).

    If packaging is wet, torn, punctured, expired, or questionable in any way: do not use it.

    Opening a sterile package

    Ordered sequence

    Eight steps in order, from the integrity check to the habit that closes it out.

    Choose the next correct step
    Your sequence so far
      Package opened safely

      Check, set up, open away from you, sides, near flap last, present without reaching over, keep it inside the border and in sight — and if anything is doubtful, replace it and say so out loud.

      Maintaining a sterile field

      Sterile touches sterile; everything else is contaminated

      Keep sterile items above waist level and in sight. Keep the field dry, because moisture can transfer microorganisms. Do not turn away from an open sterile field unless a team member is monitoring it according to protocol. Do not reach, talk into, cough over, lean on, or pass nonsterile items over the field. Replace contaminated items immediately.

      Public sterile-field guidance identifies the common contaminated areas: the border, objects below waist level, unmonitored fields, and fields compromised by holes, tears, or moisture (NCBI Bookshelf aseptic technique; OpenStax sterile technique). Sterile fields are prepared as close as possible to the time of use (AORN key takeaways).

      Sterile-field danger signs

      Click to reveal

      Six signs that a sterile item or field is no longer reliable. Open each one to see why and what to do about it.

      Wet

      A drape, wrapper, or pack that is damp or has fluid soaked through it.

      Moisture can transfer microorganisms through the barrier, so a wet field or package is treated as compromised.

      Do: stop, say so out loud, and replace the item or field per protocol.

      Torn or punctured

      A wrapper with a tear, a hole, or a puncture — however small.

      Packaging integrity is part of sterility. A breach in the wrapper is a breach in the barrier.

      Do: do not use it. Set it aside and replace it.

      Below waist level

      A sterile item or a sterile-gloved hand that has dropped below the level of the field.

      Sterile items are kept above waist level and in sight. Below that, they are treated as contaminated because they cannot be monitored.

      Do: treat it as contaminated and replace it.

      Out of sight

      An open field that nobody is watching, or one that was turned away from.

      An unmonitored sterile field is treated as compromised. There is no universal time allowance for how long a field may sit unwatched.

      Do: follow the approved covering and monitoring protocol, or treat the field as questionable and correct it.

      Touched by anything nonsterile

      A sterile item that has contacted a wrapper, a counter, a sleeve, a bare hand, or the floor.

      Sterile touches sterile. Anything else is contaminated, and duration does not matter.

      Do: remove the item from use, replace it, and tell the team.

      Unknown status

      A pack, set, or field whose processing or handling history you cannot verify.

      This is the no-mystery-item standard. Unknown is not the same as probably fine.

      Do: do not use it until the status is verified by the responsible team member.

      Sterile-field boundary map

      Sterile-field map

      Eight zones around one sterile setup. Mark every zone that is contaminated, then check the field. Three zones are sterile — marking those is its own kind of error, because it suggests the sterile working area cannot be trusted.

      Sterile field — mark the contaminated zones. Sterile touches sterile; anything else is contaminated.

      Field read correctly

      The border, anything below waist level, wet areas, an unmonitored field, and the outside of any wrapper are all contaminated. The center, sterile-gloved hands held above the waist and in view, and an item presented without reaching over the field are sterile.

      Required scenario 1 — sterile glove touches a nonsterile surface

      Required scenario

      Choose the safest action. After you choose, the panel explains your answer and why each alternative is not appropriate.

      • Scenario 1 — sterile glove touches a nonsterile surface

        You are helping set up for a sterile procedure. After donning sterile gloves, your right sterile glove brushes the outside edge of a nonsterile supply wrapper. The Pet is not yet prepped. What should you do?

      Practice complete

      Sharps and medical waste

      Point of use, upright, below the fill line, per the rules that apply where you work

      Activate safety features when they are present and you are trained. Do not recap needles unless a specific approved procedure requires it. Dispose of sharps at point of use in an approved container. Keep containers upright, accessible, not overfilled, and away from Member and Pet access. Follow Hannah, state, and local regulated medical-waste rules for blood-contaminated waste, isolation waste, pharmaceuticals, and sharps (CDC injection safety; OSHA sharps safety; OSHA bloodborne pathogens standards).

      Container types, labeling, pickup, and waste categories are set by state, local, and Hannah policy. This lesson will not assign a category for you.

      Sharps and waste decisions

      Paged decisions

      Three decisions on disposal, container status, and waste streams. Each answer explains why the alternatives are not appropriate.

      • Sharps at point of use

        You have just given an injection. The sharps container is across the treatment room. What do you do?

      • Container status

        The sharps container in the treatment area is filled past the fill line and is sitting on the floor near the kennel run.

      • Regulated waste

        You are cleaning up after a procedure that produced blood-contaminated gauze, an empty medication vial, and general packaging.

      Practice complete

      Sources for this module+
      • CDC — Preventing Unsafe Injection Practices
      • CDC — Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
      • CDC — Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices
      • OpenStax — Sterile Technique
      • NCBI Bookshelf — Chapter 4, Aseptic Technique
      • AORN — 4 Sterile Technique Questions Answered
      • AORN — Key Takeaways: Guideline for Sterile Technique
      • OSHA — Sharps Safety
      • OSHA — Bloodborne Pathogens Standards
      • CDC — Considerations for Blood Glucose Monitoring and Insulin Administration

modules.title: Fix the Breach and Knowledge Check
modules.content:
Breaches happen in every hospital. What separates a safe team from an unsafe one is what happens in the next ten seconds. This module gives you one response pattern that works for hands, surfaces, equipment, prepared sites, and sterile fields.

Asepsis scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Check the risk before touching a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument.
  • Clean hands, change gloves, and use the PPE the task and protocol call for.
  • Clean before disinfecting and keep surfaces wet for the full label contact time.
  • Stop and speak up the moment anything is questionable — any role, any time.

No one does

  • Invent a dilution, a contact time, a skin-prep recipe, an isolation category, or a waste rule.
  • Reuse, "wipe sterile," or spray a contaminated item back into service.
  • Move equipment or supplies from one Pet to another without approved processing.
  • Perform an invasive or role-restricted procedure without the required credential and DVM or RVT direction.

Universal principle, then Hannah protocol, then ask if unsure. The product label and safety data sheet, Hannah protocols, state and local rules, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable step: dilution, contact time, PPE, skin prep, isolation category, and waste handling. Disinfectant labels are legally enforceable use directions (EPA — pesticide labels), and infection-prevention programs run on written SOPs, training, and evaluation (AAHA ICPB Guidelines).

In this module you will

  • Apply one universal breach response: stop, protect, name, correct, clean hands, notify, document.
  • Recognize and correct the six required breach scenarios.
  • Recite the ten Hannah Standards in Practice and say what each one changes about your day.
  • Complete the progressive recap and the competency self-check.
  • Print the one-page C.L.E.A.N. Path job aid for your work area.

The universal breach response

Seven steps, in this order, every time

AORN-related summaries emphasize correcting breaks in sterile technique immediately unless doing so would endanger the patient (Implementing AORN recommended practices). AORN public guidance also states that when a contaminated instrument or item is found, the affected items are removed and contacted items and gloves are addressed according to the situation (AORN sterile-technique questions answered).

The habit is what makes it fast: the same seven steps whether the breach is a glove, a surface, a set, a prepared site, or a field.

Breach-response sequence

Ordered sequence

Seven steps in order. A step chosen too early explains why it comes later.

Choose the next correct step
Your sequence so far
    Breach response complete

    Stop, protect, name it clearly, correct it, clean hands and change gloves, notify, document and escalate. Repetition is the point: this should become automatic, in every room, for every role.

    Required scenario 6 — break in surgical sterility

    Required scenario

    Choose the safest response. After you choose, the panel explains your answer and why each alternative is not appropriate.

    • Scenario 6 — break in surgical sterility

      During surgery, a sterile instrument slips off the sterile field and lands on the floor. The procedure is still in progress. What should happen?

    Practice complete

    Surgical break — the full four decisions

    Branching case

    The same event, decision by decision, from the announcement to the documentation. Wrong choices explain themselves and stay available.

    Decision 1 — the instrument hits the floor

    During surgery, a sterile instrument slips off the sterile field and lands on the floor. The procedure is still in progress. What happens first?

    Decision 2 — the item itself

    The team has heard you. What happens to that instrument?

    Decision 3 — the field and the Pet

    The instrument is out of use. What about the field and the Pet?

    Decision 4 — afterwards

    The procedure is complete. What closes the loop on the breach?

    Actions you have taken
      Break handled correctly

      Announced out loud, item removed and replaced, field protected while the DVM and surgical team directed the next steps, and the breach documented and escalated per protocol.

      Hannah Standards in Practice

      Ten standards that decide the close calls

      1. Stop-the-lineAny team member may stop a task when asepsis, sterility, sharps safety, isolation, or chemical safety is uncertain. Role and credential decide who performs a procedure; they never decide who may speak up.
      2. Clean to dirtyWork from clean areas to contaminated areas, and never return to clean supplies with contaminated gloves or hands.
      3. No shortcutDo not shorten label contact time, change dilution, skip cleaning, reuse single-use supplies, or “wipe sterile” a contaminated item.
      4. No mystery itemIf the status of a package, instrument, field, medication-prep area, device, or supply is unknown, it is not used until it is verified.
      5. One Pet, one clean pathEquipment and supplies used on one Pet do not move to another Pet without approved cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, or disposal.
      6. Isolation earlySuspected contagious disease triggers early separation, limited traffic, dedicated or disinfected equipment, PPE per protocol, and clinical lead notification.
      7. Sharps at point of useUsed needles, syringes, lancets, and blades go directly into approved sharps containers at point of use.
      8. Label is the ruleProduct labels and safety data sheets govern disinfectant and chemical use: dilution, contact time, PPE, compatibility, storage, and disposal.
      9. Role boundaryFollow Hannah role expectations and DVM or RVT direction for invasive procedures, Pet skin prep, wound care, urinary catheterization, surgical prep, and isolation decisions.
      10. Ask earlyIf the next safe step is uncertain, pause and ask the responsible DVM, RVT, lead PetNurse, or hospital leadership.
      The stop phrase

      “I think this may be contaminated. Let us pause and replace, re-prep, or check protocol.”

      It is short on purpose. It names the concern, it proposes a next step, and it blames nobody. Any role can say it to any other role, at any point in any procedure.

      Never carry it forward — five rapid prompts

      Rapid recap

      Five quick decisions across hands, equipment, surfaces, fields, and speaking up. Each answer explains why the alternatives are not appropriate.

      • Rapid prompt 1 — hands

        You have just removed gloves after a fecal cleanup and your hands are visibly soiled. What is the next safe action?

      • Rapid prompt 2 — equipment

        The thermometer you just used on a Pet with diarrhea is in your hand and the next Pet is waiting. What is the next safe action?

      • Rapid prompt 3 — surfaces

        The disinfectant on the exam table dried before the label contact time was complete. What is the next safe action?

      • Rapid prompt 4 — the field

        A sterile pack was opened, then the room was left with no protocol-approved covering or monitoring. What is the next safe action?

      • Rapid prompt 5 — speaking up

      Progressive recap — the whole lesson in ten points

      Step-through recap

      Step through the C.L.E.A.N. Path and the response habits one point at a time. Move back and forth as much as you like.

      • C — Check the risk

        Before you touch a Pet, a surface, a supply, or an instrument: what could be infectious, sterile, sharp, or chemical here? Pet status, task status, space status. Standard precautions apply to every Pet, and PPE is chosen by risk assessment.

      • L — Lower the load

        Remove waste, linens, and visible soil first. Clean before you disinfect and before anything is sterilized. Keep used instruments contained so soil does not dry on them.

      • E — Establish barriers

        Hand hygiene at the right moments, gloves and PPE by risk, dedicated or processed equipment between Pets, protected sterile fields, sharps containers at point of use, traffic control, isolation barriers. PPE is the last barrier, not the only one.

      • A — Apply the rule

        The label and SDS give you dilution, wet contact time, PPE, ventilation, surface, and storage. Hannah protocol gives you the room reset, the kennel sequence, isolation, surgery, catheter, wound, and waste steps. The DVM or RVT gives you the procedure-specific prep.

      • N — Never carry contamination forward

        Change gloves, clean hands, replace contaminated sterile items, re-prep or re-clean when something was touched or dried early, dispose of sharps at point of use, and report the breach.

      • Clean is not sterile

        Cleaning removes soil. Disinfection kills many or most microorganisms depending on product and level. Sterilization destroys all of them and is required for critical items entering sterile tissue or the vascular system.

      • Hand hygiene has six moments

        Before Pet contact. Before an aseptic task. Dirty to clean on the same Pet. After the Pet or its surroundings. After blood, body fluids, waste, or contaminated surfaces. Immediately after glove removal. Soap and water when visibly soiled.

      • Sterility is binary in practice

        Wet, torn, punctured, below waist level, out of sight, touched by anything nonsterile, opened too early without approved covering, or unknown status — all of it is treated as contaminated and replaced or corrected per protocol.

      • Isolation starts on suspicion

        Acute vomiting or diarrhea, respiratory signs with exposure risk, draining wounds, suspected zoonotic risk, or an unusual cluster: separate early, limit traffic, use dedicated or disinfected equipment, PPE per protocol, and notify the clinical lead.

      • The breach response never changes

        Stop. Protect. Name it. Correct it. Clean hands and change gloves. Notify. Document and escalate per protocol. If you are unsure whether something is clean or sterile, stop and ask. Protecting every Pet begins with preventing contamination.

      Summary

      The short version

      Asepsis means preventing contamination before it reaches the next Pet, team member, supply, surface, instrument, or sterile field. Use the Hannah C.L.E.A.N. Path: Check the risk, Lower the load, Establish barriers, Apply the rule, and Never carry contamination forward. Clean hands at the right moments, change gloves when they become contaminated, clean before disinfecting, follow every product label, protect sterile fields, and speak up the moment something becomes questionable.

      If you are unsure whether something is clean or sterile, stop and ask. Protecting every Pet begins with preventing contamination.

      Ten questions, mixed format, 80 percent to pass

      Before you begin

      How this knowledge check works

      Questions appear one at a time with a progress indicator. After you answer, you get an explanation of your own answer and an explanation of why each of the other options is not appropriate. You can move back through questions you have already answered. Nothing is timed.

      The pass mark for this knowledge check is 80 percent. That threshold applies to this knowledge check only — it is not a universal Hannah threshold, and it does not replace your hospital’s competency policy, your state or local rules, or DVM and RVT direction.

      If you score below 80 percent, the remediation panel names the domains you missed and the modules to revisit: review modules 2, 4, 5, and 7, repeat the six required scenarios, and retake the check. Missing a critical domain — hand hygiene, sterile-field break, PPE and isolation, disinfectant label and contact time, or sharps and waste safety — requires remediation before you perform those tasks unsupervised, regardless of the overall percentage.

      What these questions test

      Every item tests application, not memorized product numbers. quiz.q: Q1 · Medical vs surgical asepsis · Multiple choiceWhich example best represents surgical asepsis?
opts: Washing hands after removing gloves.
Taking trash out of the exam room.
Using sterile gloves and sterile instruments while maintaining a sterile field for an invasive procedure.
Wiping an exam table after a Pet leaves.
quiz.exp: Surgical asepsis aims to keep items and the field sterile during invasive procedures.

quiz.q: Q2 · Hands and sanitizer · True or falseAlcohol-based hand sanitizer is always the best option, even when hands are visibly dirty or soiled with body fluids.
opts: True
False
quiz.exp: Soap and water are required when hands are visibly dirty or soiled, and sanitizer is preferred for many routine clinical moments when hands are not visibly soiled.

quiz.q: Q3 · Disinfectant contact time · Multiple choiceA disinfectant label requires the surface to remain wet for its contact time. The surface dries early. What should you do?
opts: Reapply product so the surface stays wet for the full label-required contact time.
Consider it disinfected because product touched the surface.
Add water to stretch the product.
Wipe with a dry towel to finish faster.
quiz.exp: This follows label-based disinfection with no invented shortcut.

The field remains sterile because no one touched it.

A clean paper form on a clipboard that stayed outside the exam room.
